ASRSN:2152830.n: During our preflight for Aircraft X, we received a notification of Dangerous Goods (DG). We received the final notification of the DG and acknowledged it. While taxiing out, we got another notification of DG, which appeared to have one of the three items removed. We acknowledged this change. Approximately 40 minutes into the flight, we received a third notification stating that the removed item had been reloaded onto the aircraft. Dispatch confirmed that the item was indeed on board.
ASRSN:2152830.s: The flight crew received three conflicting Dangerous Goods notifications for Aircraft X during preflight, taxi, and en route phases. Dispatch confirmed that an item previously reported as removed was actually reloaded and remained on board during the flight.

ASRSN:2152834.n: Prior to brake release the final Dangerous Goods (DG) was received at XA:21 and acknowledged at XA:22. Brake was released at XA:23. At XD:24 a new DG final was received with no changes from the previous. A notification form warning was received. The new final DG was acknowledged at XA:25. A third final DG was received during taxi out at XA:30. The crew reviewed the final and found no changes.
ASRSN:2152834.s: The flight crew received three final Dangerous Goods manifests prior to and during taxi out, with the last one arriving at XA:30. The crew reviewed all documents and confirmed no changes were made to the cargo load.

ASRSN:2152924.n: After landing and during taxi to ramp on taxiway 1 east of the departure end of XXL a potential safety issue was experienced. A Piper warrior departed XXL and began an immediate turn to the left. The aircraft was climbing very slowly in hot conditions and was in a nose high attitude. The aircraft flew right over our aircraft at what was estimated to be 70-80 feet. This would suggest a maximum clearance over our tail of 50- 60 feet. I was sufficiently concerned that I stopped the aircraft on the taxi way. Had we been a larger aircraft with a taller tail the situation could have been worse.
ASRSN:2152924.s: While taxiing on taxiway 1 east of XXL, the pilot stopped after a Piper Warrior departed and flew over their aircraft at an estimated 70-80 feet. The Warrior's slow climb and nose-high attitude in hot conditions resulted in a maximum tail clearance of 50-60 feet, creating a potential safety issue.

ASRSN:2152982.n: When coming into DCA we were assigned the LDA Y 19. There was weather along the route of flight. We briefed the approach and the fact that it was offset. When getting closer to DCA we got multiple vectors and were sent through the final course and back around. Eventually we were cleared for the approach. Due to a reroute we were tighter on fuel than we had originally planned for so I was a bit distracted watching that as well. Once cleared we flew the approach and when I got closer I saw the runway and turned the flight director off. At about 500 feet. Tower queried us where we were going because we were lined up with 15. We immediately went around. We came back in and requested the RNAV 19 this time to help give us better guidance. We landed safely on 19 after the go-around. Cause: Neither the First Officer (FO) or I had been to DCA before so being unfamiliar with the airport and the fact that it had been a long day full of schedule changes and sits, and the external distractions of weather and fuel concerns added to my lack of situational awareness.Suggestions: In the future when going to a new or unfamiliar airport I would double check to make sure I have a full idea of what the approach will look like and the airport diagram itself. I would also request an alternate from Dispatch going forward if the weather enroute looks bad to give us more fuel.
ASRSN:2152982.s: The crew, unfamiliar with DCA, executed a go-around at 500 feet while aligned with Runway 15 during an LDA Y 19 approach due to reduced situational awareness from weather, fuel concerns, and fatigue. They subsequently landed safely on Runway 19 after requesting an RNAV 19 approach.

ASRSN:2153021.n: On takeoff roll XXL, after takeoff thrust set and stable, Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) spiked into the red on the right engine. The N1 decreased and engine fail showed on right EGT gauge. Performed Rejected Takeoff (RTO) procedure approximately 60 knots. Ran RTO checklist, cleared the active runway, and had fire rescue inspect the right side of the aircraft and engine as a precautionary measure Taxied back to gate. After arrival, we made the Maintenance write up, called the Chief Pilot, and made sure all passengers deplaned safely. We checked on the Flight Attendants to make sure they were in good spirits. On take off roll XXL, after engines were spulled up and thrust added engines were stable . At about 60-65 knots Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) on engine number 2 spiked into the red zone. N1 decreased and engine failed depicted on the EGT engine 2. At approximately 60/65 knots we performed the Rejected takeoff (RTO) procedure, ran the RTO checklist cleared the active runway. Captain requested Fire and rescue inspection the right engine. Executed the after landing flow, and taxied to gate.
ASRSN:2153021.s: During takeoff roll on aircraft XXL, the right engine's Exhaust Gas Temperature spiked into the red and N1 decreased at 60–65 knots. The crew performed a Rejected Takeoff, cleared the runway, and taxied to the gate for a precautionary fire rescue inspection and maintenance write-up.

ASRSN:2153066.n: Holding short of Runway, we were cleared for position and hold. I push power levers up as we crossed hold short and turned on appropriate lights. That is when we smelled acrid burning rubber smell. Relief Pilot saw smoke coming from lower left section of overhead panel. We reported to tower that we needed to taxi clear of runway (since we were not cleared for takeoff yet). Once clear of runway, we completed after landing flow, as well as reviewed rejected takeoff and smoke / fumes QRC. We discussed donning O2 but symptoms had dissipated.We coordinated with ground to send fire equipment/ trucks to check us over. During that time, we coordinated with Flight Attendants (FAs) and Passengers. FAs reported smelling fumes as well, all the way back in jump seats by door 2L/R. Rescue personnel found nothing as smell dissipated an there was no more smoke being produced. Shut down engines on ground, safed" doors and rescue chief / maintenance / station manager boarded at 1L. They all reported the acrid smell as well. We decided to deboard airplane there, out of an abundance of caution. All Passengers exited thru 1L, down air stairs and bussed to terminal. At some point, we noticed runway turnoff light circuit breaker had popped. We were towed to Maintenance removed overhead panel for runway turnoff lights (lower left of overhead) and found considerable charring. Photos attached. Throughout, continuous coordination with Dispatch, station ops and Chief Pilot, and local maintenance with Maintenance Control."
ASRSN:2153066.s: The flight crew smelled burning rubber and saw smoke from the overhead panel while holding short of the runway after pushing power levers. Investigation revealed a popped runway turnoff light circuit breaker and charring in the panel, leading to a precautionary deplaning of all passengers.

ASRSN:2153078.n: Roanoke RNAV (RNP) Z Rwy 24 was loaded into the FMS procedurally correct andflown procedurally correct with the Capt flying. Between points DBERB andWILHE Roanoke Tower alerted us to a Low Altitude alert, and told us to checkour Altimeter 3005.We immediately checked our Altimeters, they were both set 3005, and we alsore-confirmed both displays and the aircraft was correct vertically andlaterally with no navigation warnings displayed. There was NO Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning (EGPWS) alert;it was Day VMC and we could ascertain that we were in a safe positionvertically and laterally with the runway in sight and the PAPI indicatingcorrectly so we continued to a safe landing.
ASRSN:2153078.s: During the Roanoke RNAV (RNP) Z approach to Runway 24, Tower issued a low altitude alert despite the crew verifying correct altimeter settings and navigation. The crew confirmed safe vertical and lateral position visually and continued to a safe landing with no EGPWS activation.

ASRSN:2153108.n: RNAV GPS RW 19 App TEB. Missed approach requires an initial 1500 MSL level off. At 500 AGL, encountered wind shear accompanied by an Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) alert. Preformed escape/go around maneuver. Climbed to 2100' MSL to escape wind shear. ATC asked us to descend to 1500'. PM advised ATC we are currently in wind shear. At no time were other aircraft required to alter flight path or altitude. Contacted departure control and was sequenced into traffic flow where a second instrument approach and landing was successful..It is certainly possible a level off at 1500' would have been adequate. In the moment, it was my decision to add an additional level of safety to the altitude required by the missed approach. In addition, I was monitoring TCAS for conflicts.
ASRSN:2153108.s: During an RNAV GPS RW 19 approach at TEB, the crew encountered wind shear and an EGPWS alert at 500 AGL, prompting a go-around to 2100' MSL. The pilot voluntarily climbed above the required 1500' missed approach level for safety, coordinated with ATC, and completed a successful second landing.

ASRSN:2153122.n: L/G Landing Gear Control Interface Unit (LGCIU) 1FAULT on dept from ZZZ enroute to ZZZ1 AFTER COMPLETING QRH PROCEDURES COULD NOT DETERMINE STATUS OF GEAR BECAUSE ALL 6 lights remained on 3 red unlock and 3 green down and locked lites on..after consulting with dispatch an Maintenance Control we determined to lower gear and if it came down and locked we would divert to ZZZ2. It did we briefed pax's and fa vehicles were summoned and made uneventful landing on XXL in ZZZ2 had them inspect plane and cleared runway and they followed us to gate.Suggestion: Better QRH procedures for this malfunction.
ASRSN:2153122.s: The crew experienced an LGCIU 1 fault en route, leaving all six landing gear lights illuminated despite QRH procedures. They diverted to ZZZ2, where the gear locked, allowing an uneventful landing and subsequent inspection.

ASRSN:2153132.n: Normal taxi to runway for departure. After takeoff clearance was received I stabilized the engines at 40% N1. Hit TOGA and the engines symmetrically advanced to the takeoff power setting. As we accelerated the aircraft began to deviate to the right. I added more and more left rudder but was unable to arrest the right deviation. Below 40 knots I rejected the takeoff and brought the aircraft to a stop on the runway. At not point did the aircraft leave the runway surface. We taxied clear of the runway and returned to the gate where a Logbook entry was made.
ASRSN:2153132.s: The pilot rejected the takeoff below 40 knots after the aircraft deviated right despite full left rudder input. The cause was attributed to an inability to arrest the deviation, resulting in a safe stop on the runway and a subsequent logbook entry.

ASRSN:2153170.n: I was pilot flying (PF) and we were descending to 10,000 via the Powda One STAR. The approach briefing was to expect a visual approach to runway 12, which we would back up with the ILS-12. The pilot monitoring (PM) checked in with approach control descending to 10,000 via the Powda One. As planned, the PM subsequently requested the ILS-12, KICDO (IAF) transition after the STAR. The response was a casual, 'That's approved, and you can go direct KICDO at this time.' We turned direct KICDO and continued descent to 10,000. In VMC conditions of clear skies and unlimited visibility, out of 11,000 descending to 10,000, we recognized the altitude would be close to a distant peak off the left of the nose which was verified by the PM as 9;650ft. As we decided we needed to go back to 11,000, the approach controller called sounding confused and climbed us to 11,000 with a 20 degree right turn. This was immediately followed up with a turn to 300deg and seconds later a turn to 360deg. After reaching the 360 heading we were descended back to 10,000 before we had even reached 11,000 and within a minute we were given direct KICDO. Due to the flight conditions and our awareness of the surrounding terrain, at no time was the aircraft in danger of a terrain alert. Cause: This event was caused by being cleared direct to a fix off the STAR without an associated altitude clearance. Suggestion: Proactively requesting a new altitude clearance when cleared off a published route which was governing our descent or climb. We were flying the POWDA ONE RNAV arrival transitioning to the ILS Rwy 12. On the arrival we were given a descend via clearance, selected the lowest altitude of 10000, and selected VNAV. While on the arrival we told the Controller we wanted to fly the ILS from the IAF named KICDO. From KICDO there is an arcing transition to the final approach course. The Controller cleared us direct to KICDO. Since we were pulled off the arrival we were no longer on the descend via portion and still had 10000 in the altitude selector. At this point we should have been at 11000 to adequately clear terrain in front of us. We had leveled at 10000. I looked again at the chart and we agreed we needed to climb to 11000 and started a climb. It should be noted that we were in VMC conditions and had visual confirmation of the terrain. At that moment the Controller also wondered why we were at 10000 ft. I said we agreed with her and were in the climb to 11000. She was happy with that and turned us to the right for a radar vector. After a couple additional heading changes we intercepted the ILS course and made a normal approach and landing.Cause: Staying in a VNAV descent while being pulled off a charted route and not confirming an altitude assignment.Suggestion: When deviating from a charted route with prescribed altitudes at along track fixes, obtain and confirm an altitude assignment from ATC.
ASRSN:2153170.s: The pilot flying and pilot monitoring descended to 10,000 feet on the Powda One STAR before being cleared direct to KICDO without a new altitude assignment. This caused a temporary descent below the required 11,000 feet terrain clearance, prompting a climb and radar vectors until the ILS approach was safely intercepted.

ASRSN:2153249.n: In the climb phase about 15 minutes after departure we got an engine 1 overheat light annunciation. We advised ATC of the situation and let them know we wanted a vector towards ZZZZ airport. We ran the immediate action items and the checklist. I flew the plane and talked on the radios as the Captain coordinated with dispatch and Maintenance Control.We [requested priority] and shot the ILS Runway XXL in ZZZZ with reduced thrust in the #1 engine. We had an uneventful landing and pulled off the active runway. We set the parking brake and requested inspection of the engine prior to taxiing back to the gate. Flight Attendants and Passengers were kept informed throughout the entire situation. Eng 1 Overheat came on in climb passing 13000 ft. We performed the immediate action items, then QRC and QRH. We leveled off at 17000 ft. and coordinated for a turn back towards ZZZZ airport. We called Dispatch who included Maintenance Control per Flight Manual (FM). We concluded [requesting priority handling] and returning to ZZZZ airport was warranted. While I was on the radios, the FO flew the jet. We opted to land overweight since we had a long runway. We landed uneventfully and had crash fire rescue look us over before we taxied to park. After discussing it, we opted to taxi in with the left motor shut down and the right motor running (non-standard) due to possible overheating on left motor if we used it for taxi. No issues on the taxi back to parking.The flight was cancelled by operations after about an hour in chalks.
ASRSN:2153249.s: During climb at 13,000 ft, the crew received an Engine 1 overheat light, returned to ZZZZ airport, and landed uneventfully with reduced thrust. They taxied back with Engine 1 shut down to prevent overheating, after which operations cancelled the flight.

ASRSN:2153257.n: About 15 minutes into cruise/45 minutes into the flight Auto pilot disengaged. There were Master cautions for speed trim fail (single channel failure), and a right Internal Reference System (IRS) fault. The FO side lost attitude and heading information. The Flight Manual (FM) QRH instructed to disengage auto pilot, and the auto throttle. Both IRS's were put onto the left side. We [requested priority] for loss of a navigation system. We descended to FL270 to exit RVSM airspace because of the loss of auto pilot. After coordinating with dispatch and maintenance, a decision was made to divert to ZZZ1 (instead of returning to ZZZ) there was better weather at that field, and it allowed us to burn off some more gas as to not have as high of an overweight landing. An overweight landing was made at approximately 164,000 lbs. We parked at the gate with no further complications.
ASRSN:2153257.s: During cruise, the crew experienced an autopilot disengagement, speed trim failure, and right IRS fault, causing loss of FO attitude and heading. They descended to FL270 to exit RVSM airspace and diverted to ZZZ1 for an overweight landing of 164,000 lbs due to better weather and fuel considerations.

ASRSN:2153265.n: After landing in SAN in night/VMC conditions we cleared the active runway onto B taxiway and were handed off to Ramp Control. We were told to taxi Bravo to the Bravo hold line. At the end of Bravo there were a line of aircraft off to the left of the taxiway waiting to park. We interrupted the instructions to get in line behind the aircraft which we did. The Ramp Controller then asked us to make a 180 and follow the line to the Bravo hold line. There was no Bravo hold line depicted on the 10-9 but we found there was on the Airport Moving Map (AMM). We complied with instructions and there were no issues. However, it did bring to attention that the Bravo hold line was not depicted on the 10-9 and the line leading to the Bravo hold line was part of the West Ramp and not labeled as part of the Bravo taxiway. As we exited Runway 27, Ramp Control cleared us to 'taxi on B past Spot One Holding Point Bravo.' Both the FO and I took that to mean to taxi past Spot One, then hold short of Bravo. We passed Spot One and got in line behind the other waiting aircraft. We were told to turn back around and continue taxiing past Spot One. It wasn't until we found Holding Point Bravo on the pavement that we understood. There is no Holding Point Bravo depicted on the -9 page. It is depicted on the Airport Moving Map (AMM) page with nonstandard markings and a very small letter.
ASRSN:2153265.s: The flight crew experienced confusion while taxiing at SAN after landing due to a missing Bravo hold line on the 10-9 chart. Although the hold line appeared on the Airport Moving Map, the crew initially misinterpreted Ramp Control instructions, requiring a 180-degree turn to reach the correct position.

ASRSN:2153280.n: MX preformed a TR (Tail Rotor) track and balance on Day 0 when they removed their equipment, they failed to replace the bolts that held that equipment on the T/R gearbox. On Day 2 while pre-flighting the helicopter I wrote up the starter light, the helicopter was out of sight (OOS) for the next 2 days. On Day 4 after pre flight I received 4 patient flights through out the day. On Day 5 I was notified that MX found 2 missing bolts on the T/R they failed to replace after they removed the T/R vibe gear. Suggestions: MX that did the Required Inspection Item (RII) should be more diligent on their checks and the new mechanic needs to ask more questions on what should be replaced after removal of testing equipment. Less pressure on MX to get the helicopter back in service because managers are worried about there OOS times because they affect their KPI's (Key Performance Indicators). Torque stripping bolts to make them easier to see on walk arounds. I'll be looking at all bolts and fasteners during walk arounds.
ASRSN:2153280.s: Maintenance personnel failed to replace two bolts on the tail rotor gearbox after removing test equipment, causing the helicopter to be out of service for two days. The missing bolts were discovered on Day 5, prompting the pilot to inspect all fasteners and suggesting reduced pressure on mechanics to improve inspection diligence.

ASRSN:2153289.n: Aircraft: Aircraft X (A319), Aircraft Y (A321)This report details two separate incidents involving two aircraft, during which I encountered damaged or missing wing seals. I experienced significant pressure from management to alter my documentation, which I believe may compromise safety standards.Aircraft X Day 0 During a routine pre-flight inspection, I documented a total of 7 damaged or missing Slat End Seals, with damage observed on both wings.The aircraft was placed out of service by maintenance for necessary repairs as the A320 fleet CDL (Configuration Deviation List) manual permits only 1 wing seal per wing to be deferred at a time. This action was taken to ensure compliance with safety standards and maintenance procedures.Aircraft Y Day 0 During a subsequent pre-flight inspection of this aircraft, I identified 2 damaged wing seals on the right wing, 1 Slat End Seal and 1 Inboard Aileron Edge to Wing Seal.During this discovery, I was approached by a Supervisor and Chief Pilot. Chief Pilot approached me during the walk-around inspection and asked me to explain the issue and if I had a mechanic background. Chief Pilot indicated the necessity of moving passengers and questioned how many seals I would document. I replied that I will document 2 seals on the right wing. From inside the aircraft, Supervisor stopped me from documenting the discrepancies and indicated the necessity of moving passengers. Supervisor implied that if I continued to put aircraft out of service there would be serious implications and made a reference to 'arrangements' and the negative connotation associated with upper management.Feeling pressured by these comments and concerned about potential disciplinary action or termination, I documented only 1 of the 2 damaged seals on the right wing of Aircraft Y, despite the presence of multiple discrepancies. I will not succumb to the pressure again and fail to document a mechanical discrepancy. I have reported these issues in accordance with standard procedures and safety guidelines. However, the undue pressure from management to underreport the number of damaged seals on Aircraft Y has raised concerns about potential retaliation and compromised safety. Also, I am concerned that management may be pressuring other pilots - as evidenced by the aircraft that are accepted with this issue. Additionally, this may be a broader problem of management trading safety for on-time/cancelation due to pressure from DOT regulations. I am reporting this matter to ensure that proper safety protocols are followed and to address the pressures that may impact the accurate reporting of mechanical discrepancies. Damaged wing seals are an A320 fleet wide problem at Company X and must be resolved. Cause: On Day 0 I was approached at the aircraft while performing pre-flight duties by 2 of company members of management who pressured me to overlook mechanical discrepancies in order to keep aircraft flying. Interfering with the Captain's Part 121 regulatory duties by making threatening comments and implying potential disciplinary action and/or termination of employment is at the highest level of unconscionable conduct by a Part 121 operator. I recommend that an organization proceed with a formal investigation of the events that occurred on Day 0 and associated corporate cultural issues that may reduce safety standards at company.
ASRSN:2153289.s: A pilot reported that management pressured them to underreport damaged wing seals on an A319 and A321 during pre-flight inspections to avoid delays. Consequently, the pilot documented only one of two discrepancies on the A321 despite safety concerns, citing threats of disciplinary action and a culture prioritizing on-time performance over safety.

ASRSN:2153293.n: Finished deviating around weather and was then cleared direct DRAKE." No mention or specification by the controller as to whether or not it was a VOR or an intersection. Believe it or not there are actually both DRK VOR and DRAKE intersection, both located in the southwestern USA.Two fixes with the same "name" - as in spoken name. One of the two, DRAKE or DRK, needs to be renamed so as to eliminate the obvious confusion."
ASRSN:2153293.s: The pilot reported confusion after being cleared direct DRAKE, as both a DRK VOR and a DRAKE intersection share the same spoken name in the southwestern USA. The reporter recommends renaming one fix to eliminate this ambiguity.

ASRSN:2153308.n: The aircraft was located at a handstand. Took the bus to the aircraft, boarded and began aircraft preflight duties. Once aircraft doors were closed, informed ground personnel we were ready to go. He said that I was clear to release the brakes. As I did that, the fo informed me that clearance had given us a wheels up time of an hour later. I informed the ground guy and we sat there at the handstand for an hour. Once clearance had informed us we were clear to start, I once again informed the ground guy and he said that we were clear to start. Important note: this hard stand was one that you can just taxi straight out of. I had never been on one of these and it didn't really register initially in my head that we had no tug attached. When he cleared us to start, I then realized that was how this worked and I told the fo he could start the engines. Just as the engines were started, the ground guy starting telling us to stop, stop, stop. I wasn't sure what he meant and told the fo to cut the engines off. It was at that time that I realized we were rolling forward and immediately hit the brakes. We had only rolled a few feet. No one was injured and nothing was hit. Cause: Assumptions and routine were the causal factors here. The ground personnel routinely clear us to release brakes when we are ready for departure, and we do the same. Neither of us really gave any thought to the fact that this was a special circumstance that required the brakes to remain set. I, initially thinking that we might be pushed, and not correctly assessing the uniqueness of this particular hard stand, was easily drawn into what could have been a dire circumstance. Thank God nothing happened. Only a lesson learned.
ASRSN:2153308.s: The pilot and ground personnel at a unique hard stand released brakes and started engines based on routine assumptions, causing the aircraft to roll forward a few feet. The pilot immediately applied brakes, preventing injury or damage, attributing the incident to failing to recognize the specific stand required brakes to remain set without a tug.

ASRSN:2153330.n: On departure out of ZZZ we noticed a crack and arching on the left-hand side, captain side windscreen. We ran a checklist and was informed by the Flight Attendant that they smelt a burning smell in the back. I decided to [request priority] and diverted to ZZZ1.Cause: Initially, I decided to continue to ZZZ2, but I tried to reach out to Dispatch for a maintenance patch on 129.4 through company. Communications were unreadable so I tried 129.9 and was unable to connect with dispatch. I made the decision to divert to ZZZ1.Suggestions: Check to make sure that connection with Company is reliable. Flight ZZZ-ZZZ2 on Date 0.Everything was normal until we were climbing through ~24,000 ft. I was PF, CA was PM. I noticed a sudden crack had developed on the CA side windshield. Immediately following this we witnessed arcing occur in the cracked area moving from bottom to top. We decided to level off at FL240. I flew and took the radios while the CA ran through the QRH. CA also attempted to contact company through several means without success. Several minutes after the initial level off the FA's called and noted a burning smell from the cabin. We discussed our options and decided on [requesting priority] and diverting to ZZZ1. As we made our way to ZZZ1 we elected to descend at 1000 FPM for pressurization concerns. CA did get in contact with the company enroute to ZZZ1. ATC gave us vectors for the visual XXL as we made our way down. We landed and taxied to the gate without any further issue.Cause: Maintenance related issue with CA side windshield.
ASRSN:2153330.s: During climb through 24,000 ft, the pilot flying observed a crack and arcing on the captain's side windshield, followed by a burning smell reported by cabin crew. The crew leveled off, requested priority, and diverted to ZZZ1 due to a maintenance-related windshield failure.

ASRSN:2153494.n: Flying live pax leg into ZZZ, slat/flap malfunction, slat, flap, Kruger all failed to come down. Request vectors and to maintain altitude. Decided to divert to ZZZ1 a requested longest runway. Proceeded to run checklists with delayed vectors into ZZZ1. Landed RWY XXR and proceeded to the ramp on our power.
ASRSN:2153494.s: The flight crew experienced a slat, flap, and Kruger failure during the approach to ZZZ. They diverted to ZZZ1, landed on runway XXR, and taxied to the ramp under their own power.

ASRSN:2153500.n: At approximately XA:30 (L), a Cessna 177 Cardinal taxied onto Runway XX while a flight school aircraft was still on the runway, preparing to exit at taxiway 1. Although the Cardinal saw the Piper Cherokee and waited for it to clear the runway before starting his takeoff procedures, he did not notice another Piper Cherokee on short final. This oversight led the Piper Cherokee on short final to perform a go-around for safety.
ASRSN:2153500.s: A Cessna 177 Cardinal taxied onto Runway XX while a flight school aircraft was exiting, but the pilot failed to see a second Piper Cherokee on short final. This oversight caused the landing Cherokee to execute a go-around for safety.

ASRSN:2153515.n: I was doing a local training flight with a student. We did some maneuvers after leaving our home airport and practiced some landings at ZZZ as well. Before heading to ZZZ, I gave my student a simulated engine failure. I wasn't sure whether or not the student was going to make the field he was simulating he would land in if the engine failure was a real life situation. I had the student continue to try to make the field and I let the student get too low before telling them to apply full power and go-around. In the future when practicing with students, I will not let them get below the MSAs from the FARs and instruct them to add power and go-around a few hundred feet before reaching our minimum safe altitude, creating a cushion of altitude so this mistake never happens again.
ASRSN:2153515.s: An instructor and student conducting local training at ZZZ experienced a simulated engine failure where the student descended too low before executing a go-around. The instructor attributed the incident to allowing the student to fly below Minimum Safe Altitudes and plans to enforce earlier go-arounds in future training.

ASRSN:2153529.n: I was the Captain and Pilot Flying an FAR 135 flight on an IFR flight plan in VMC conditions from TYQ to PTK. Approaching PTK, we noticed multiple targets on our TCAS display within 2000 ft. of our assigned altitude of 5000 MSL mostly below us, some within 3 miles and 400 ft. below. ATC gave us traffic advisories several times, which we responded to as 'looking for traffic.' The First Officer saw the intruding traffic before I did, and at the same time the TCAS ordered a climb RA, he said 'climb'. As the TCAS slowed the climb rate and said to level off, we complied and still had the traffic in sight. In doing so, we leveled off close to 6000 ft. When clear of conflict we verified altitude with ATC, and descended to 5000 again. Then within the next 30 seconds we received a TA, followed by immediate ATC instructions to change heading and altitude. We complied expeditiously and did not receive a second RA. Both conflicting aircraft were noted to be local flight school aircraft. All of these conflicts were between 21NM to 10NM southwest of PTK. After that, the flight resumed as normal, and we completed a visual approach to Runway 27L at PTK. ATC did an outstanding job of assisting with locating non-participating aircraft in Class E airspace under the overlying Detroit Class Bravo shelf. Aside from actually putting eyes on the other traffic, I'm not sure there's much else we could have done. We worked well as a crew today, and were both aware of the amount of traffic on the TCAS display. Sim training prepared us well for this particular flight and scenario. It felt like a textbook training event we had both seen before.
ASRSN:2153529.s: The Captain and First Officer of an FAR 135 flight encountered multiple flight school aircraft near PTK, triggering a TCAS climb Resolution Advisory at 5000 feet. The crew executed the climb to 6000 feet, followed ATC heading and altitude changes, and completed a visual approach to Runway 27L without further conflict.

ASRSN:2153531.n: While on a solo pattern flight on touchdown the plane started to veer left from left turning tendencies, tried to correct with rudders however the plane kept pulling. Took a corner of intersection onto taxiway before coming to a halt. No damage or injury to plane or pilot, no other aircraft were near taxiway or intersection. Debriefing with CFI to go over controlling aircraft even after landing, and talked about the importance of rudder inputs when dealing with left turning tendencies.
ASRSN:2153531.s: A solo pilot experienced left-turning tendencies on touchdown during a pattern flight, causing the aircraft to veer left despite rudder corrections. The plane exited the runway onto a taxiway intersection before stopping with no damage or injury, prompting a debrief on post-landing rudder control.

ASRSN:2153551.n: I was conducting tailwheel training in my personally owned aircraft for a private pilot. The student was flying from the front seat and I was flying from the back. We were practicing crosswind wheel landings on runway XX. Winds were reported as 190/6 but wind direction was variable. The approach to landing was normal but after touchdown during the roll out, the student's left foot became stuck between the rudder pedal and heel brake. The aircraft swerved violently to the left. I put in full right rudder and brake deflection to maintain directional control but the aircraft departed the runway to the left hand side. The aircraft entered the surrounding grass area at a relatively low speed, and I was able to regain directional control to avoid a ground loop. After the aircraft came to a stop, I assessed that neither the student nor I were injured and that the aircraft was not damaged. I made a radio call to Tower and told the Controller we were okay. The Controller said we could taxi back. I requested a takeoff from present position with 3000ft of runway remaining. We were cleared to takeoff, taxied onto the runway from the grass, and took off. We remained in the pattern for two or three more landings and then departed for ZZZ1. Tower provided me a number to call as we were departing the pattern. After landing at ZZZ1, I inspected the aircraft and found no damage. However, I did discover that the front left brake and back right brake had been swapped. The heel brake consists of a post and a tab that points either left or right, depending on whether it's for the front or back seat. Because the brake pedals were swapped, the tab on the left brake interfered with where you would place your left foot for the front rudder pedal, and caused the student's foot to become stuck between the rudder and brake. The aircraft was completely restored in 2004, and the rudder pedals were most likely unknowingly installed in the wrong spots. The front left and back right brakes will be swapped so that the brake pedals do not cause any interference.I called the number Tower gave me and provided my name, address, and certificate number as requested. I also explained what caused the aircraft to depart the prepared surface. The FAA representative I talked to said that no landing lights were damaged and that they didn't observe any damage to the aircraft.
ASRSN:2153551.s: During tailwheel training in a privately owned aircraft, a student's foot became stuck between the rudder pedal and heel brake due to swapped brake pedals, causing a runway departure. The instructor regained control on the grass, and no injuries or damage occurred before the aircraft was cleared to taxi back and depart.

ASRSN:2153554.n: I was seated on the R seat of a Citation 5 jet. Next to me on the L seat was the PIC manipulating the flight controls. He was navigating through an area of convective activity and later on to what it was referred to as part of hurricane Debby. ATC had given us clearance to deviate for convective activity to the L or R of course and so we did. Our ADS-B weather in the cockpit was not indicating any big cells ahead of us but there was a small area that appeared in our radar at our 12 o'clock without much notice, which seemed to be below our flight path.As we flew through the general area, our autopilot became disconnected and we encounter mod/severe turbulence with what appeared to be hail. The aircraft loss a total of about 1300 feet in altitude but was able to recover altitude after 20-30 seconds later. Similar weather was noticed in our return flight from ZZZ on Day 0 without having the autopilot get disconnected again. The aircraft did not suffer any apparent damage and they were no injuries to any of the crew or passengers.Later on, the mechanics reported that damage was found on the cone of the nose and both wings de-icing equipment.
ASRSN:2153554.s: The PIC and co-pilot of a Citation 5 encountered severe turbulence and hail while deviating for convective activity, causing autopilot disconnection and a 1,300-foot altitude loss. Although no injuries occurred, mechanics later found damage to the nose cone and wing de-icing equipment.

ASRSN:2153555.n: Identified critically low engine oil pressure. In the process of mitigating emergency, restricted airspace was entered without prior clearance. I contacted controlling agency and was directed to exit restricted airspace. Communicated urgency of situation and request vector to nearest airport landing safely.
ASRSN:2153555.s: The pilot identified critically low engine oil pressure and entered restricted airspace without clearance while mitigating the emergency. After contacting ATC, the pilot was directed to exit the restricted area and vectored to the nearest airport for a safe landing.

ASRSN:2153575.n: While on a visual approach to Hendricks County, joining a left downwind to Runway 36. I descended from cruise at 3500 ft early to avoid Indianapolis class C airspace. I descended a little too low, causing me to be too low (approx 1750 MSL) over the Danville town and too close to the tower on the brickyard 244 radial. Instead, I should have stayed west of Danville until I was south of Danville, and then joined a mid field downwind toward a left base to Runway 36.
ASRSN:2153575.s: The pilot descended too early from 3500 ft to avoid Indianapolis Class C airspace while on a visual approach to Hendricks County Runway 36. This resulted in the aircraft being approximately 1750 MSL over Danville and too close to the tower on the brickyard 244 radial.

ASRSN:2153579.n: I was flying from ZZZ to my home base, JWN, at 4000 feet, on an IFR flight plan, and in contact with Memphis Center. Conditions in IMC were smooth and my autopilot with altitude hold was engaged. Communications with Memphis Center were 5 by 5 and the frequency congestion was light.I was told to contact Nashville Approach on XXX.X and communications deteriorated immediately to static and frequency congestion. The Nashville Controller immediately advised me of weather to my left and ahead. My iPad was connected to a Stratus ADS-B In device. No weather was painting on my iPad. No other weather was in the area, when I briefed the flight, I acknowledged ATC and advised I was IMC. I was alert for any change in conditions, and expecting rain.Seconds later my left wing dropped and I began descending in a no rain downdraft. I had to disconnect my autopilot, I leveled the wings and then applied full power. Even so, I was still descending within the downdraft. But for the descent, conditions were smooth. Maximum descent rate was 769 FPM, and averaged 335 FPM. The downdraft conditions lasted about three minutes, and I lost about 1,000 feet in total. During this period I advised ATC I was 'descending'. In retrospect I should have said 'Unable to maintain altitude.', but I had my hands full and my first priority was to get out of the downdraft with my wings level. Static still prevailed on the frequency and it was difficult to listen to calls. I did try to contact ATC several times during the descent, but did not receive a reply. I learned later the controller was coordinating my loss of altitude with Memphis Center.Once I excited the downdraft and I contacted ATC again. I was chastised, on frequency, for an extended period of time for violating separation. I offered to continue this conversation offline, and the controller cleared me direct to JWN at 3,000 feet, but then began explaining his side of the story.I have only guessed at the separation loss with the other aircraft in this report.Lesson learned: I should have said 'Unable to maintain altitude' instead of saying 'I'm descending'. My phrasing caused confusion in my communications with the controller. I also experienced a true to life lesson on the latency of ADS-B weather.An additional safety factor, affecting this flight and others, is the constant static on Nashville Approach frequencies caused my numerous radio antennas in the area.
ASRSN:2153579.s: A pilot flying IFR at 4,000 feet encountered a severe downdraft while transitioning to Nashville Approach, losing 1,000 feet despite disconnecting the autopilot. The pilot was later reprimanded for separation violations due to unclear radio phrasing and noted that ADS-B weather data failed to display the hazard.

ASRSN:2153584.n: Aircraft lost left brake actuation while under braking in the landing roll past the half-way point of the runway which prevented slowing the aircraft to a stop on the runway. The aircraft has a castering nose wheel and requires differential braking to control steering, so without equal braking only partial right brake could be used to slow the aircraft to prevent a more extreme turn to the right. Given the lack of braking control, the aircraft departed the runway at the departure end of the runway.During the runway overrun, the right wing impacted a runway end light resulting in visible damage to the composite skin on the underside of the right wing. The damage to the wing appears non-structural.To effect a complete stop, the right brake was applied fully to turn the aircraft to the right and skid to a stop once the nose wheel reached full deflection. If the aircraft had a steerable nose wheel, the right brake may have been able to stop the aircraft while maintaining directional control, but this is not possible in a castering nose wheel aircraft with a single sided brake failure.The left brake master cylinder and wheel assembly still need to be inspected to determine the cause of the failure. There was no binding or noise coming from the wheels or brakes when the aircraft was being towed back to the hangar.
ASRSN:2153584.s: The pilot reported a left brake failure during the landing roll, causing a runway overrun and right wing impact with a light due to the aircraft's castering nose wheel design. The aircraft stopped after skidding right, sustaining non-structural wing damage, while the brake failure cause remains under inspection.

ASRSN:2153591.n: My student was coming in on her 3rd or 4th solo landing on her 3rd solo flight. I wason the ramp watching when I saw she was a little low on final. Iwatched her level off and add some power to try and correct.She then landed and looked like there was little flare used in herlanding so she landed flat and fast. Next thing I know theairplane went off the runway down into the grass and then shequickly added rudder to get out of the grass. The studentthen decided to taxi back to the ramp where I was and I signaledfor her to shut the plane off. She got out I checked if she wasokay and when I knew she was I immediately secured the aircraft.
ASRSN:2153591.s: A student pilot on a solo landing approached low and fast, resulting in a flat touchdown that took the aircraft off the runway into grass. The pilot recovered by applying rudder, taxied back to the ramp, and the instructor secured the aircraft after confirming the student was uninjured.

ASRSN:2153652.n: I was the On-the-Job Training Instructor (OJTI) responsible for Local Control. Runway 19 was in use and things were normal. Aircraft Y was over the runway, PAST the threshold when Aircraft X crossing into the Runway Safety Area (RSA) and came to a stop partially over the edge line of Runway 19 at G4 intersection, to the immediate forward left of Aircraft Y. This happened without warning and was an immediate loss of runway separation, as Aircraft Y was past the threshold and very low over the runway. My trainee yelled 'stop that guy' in reference to Aircraft X, as is often the case in a situation like this. I said 'not that' as my trainee quickly switched to trying to send Aircraft Y around. My trainee started with 'Aircraft Y over the runway, go around' but also used Aircraft Y's callsign in the same/a repeated instruction at the end. Aircraft Y said they couldn't go around, so I advised them of the traffic over the edge line to their forward left, which the pilot acknowledged seeing. Aircraft Y touched down in close proximity to Aircraft X and almost certainly rolled past them on the ground. At the time of the runway incursion, Aircraft Y was past the threshold, and in the flare. After the event, the pilot of Aircraft Y advised that he 'was committed to the landing and unable to go around.' The touchdown zone on Runway 19 is before the G4 intersection and with different timing a collision was certainly possible. Light General Aviation (GA) aircraft often exit 19 at [Taxiway] B3, which is directly across from G4 and are almost always on the ground by G4. Unfortunately, from the Local Control perspective, there isn't really anything we could do with this sequence of events/timing to prevent the situation. Ground Control did not see Aircraft X violate the RSA in time to stop them. When Ground did try to stop Aircraft X, they were already in the RSA, but did not respond to instructions to stop. After we attempted to send Aircraft Y around on Local Control, we reached out to Aircraft X and they were on Tower frequency but never checked on. This is the second runway incursion at this location in just over a week. The same thing happened at G4 on Day 0 at the same location with Runway 19 active. The only difference on Day 0 was that the arriving aircraft had not yet passed the threshold and was able to go around. In both instances, I'm relatively sure that the pilots of the violating aircraft were not based here or local. Furthermore, this runway incursion has occurred multiple times over the years I have been here. The FBO's Ramp has multiple taxiway stubs/intersections that DO NOT CONNECT to a parallel/main taxiway and are VERY SHORT, pretty much only existing after the hold bar. Prior to a few years ago, the RSA was smaller and there was more Ramp space around these intersections.A few years ago, Runway 01/19 underwent construction for RSA issues. Among many changes, the Golf-side taxiways had their hold bars moved to the correct, further away RSA. This took away from the Ramp space that was there, shortening the available space to move before an aircraft would reach the RSA. The taxiways in question are G2, G3 and G4. Taxiway Golf starts at G5 and runs parallel to Runway 01/19. The reason why G4 is always an issue is that it is directly abeam the FBO Ramp. Aircraft utilizing G2 or G3 are typically the ones parked near them, and are almost always FRG-based aircraft. G4, on the other hand, is in line with the front of the FBO hangar, and aircraft are almost always parked nose-in to the hangar. When these aircraft start up and call for taxi, they are waved left - west - by marshallers, turning toward the runway and away from the hangar. With transient aircraft, this points them right at G4, with limited time and space before they reach the hold bar. We, Organization and Management at the local level, have brought this issue up with Airport Operations multiple times over the years, but have not had any success mitigating the issue. We have asked for it to be a hot spot and asked for guard lighting. Recently, both of those steps were taken for the Bravo/Alpha intersection due to runway incursions onto Runway 01. In all of my years at FRG, I believe G4 has had more issues and definitely should get the same treatment. Irrefutably, this problem has occurred twice in a very short amount of time. The layout is somewhat unusual and the only spot it occurs at FRG. Pilots go from non-movement area to RSA/'on the runway' in a matter of feet, with only a few lines of paint separating them - hold bar. At XA:20 in preparation for departing, after receiving taxi instructions from the FBO, I departed [the] FBO onto Gulf 4 taxiway to proceed to Runway 19. I saw the 'hold short line' for Runway 19 almost immediately after entering G4. I applied my brakes and stopped short of the runway. I was told to hold short of the runway. I was then told to cross 19 and turn right onto Bravo to then hold short of l9.As I waited, I was told to call the Tower either before departing or after landing at my destination. I elected to depart when permitted and fly to my destination at ZZZ. I then called the Farmingdale Tower and was told that the nose of my aircraft crossed the runway line. I had seen the incoming plane land without any difficulty. The Tower then said this problem had occurred just the previous week because of the short length of Taxiway G4 from FBO to Runway 19. The Tower said the FAA had been notified the previous week of this same problem. I felt strongly that the nose of my aircraft never crossed the runway line prior to being cleared across.
ASRSN:2153652.s: Local Control and a transient pilot experienced a runway incursion at G4 intersection on Runway 19 when the pilot crossed the Runway Safety Area while an arriving aircraft was in the flare. The pilot claimed to have stopped short of the hold line, but the tower reported the nose crossed the runway, causing a loss of separation due to the short taxiway layout.

ASRSN:2153664.n: Upon pushback from gate XX at ZZZ, the tug driver reported a breakaway of the tow bar. The Captain immediately applied the necessary braking, and stopped the aircraft. We followed FOM procedures, the aircraft was inspected, and returned to service. No further issues occurred, and we had an uneventful flight to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2153664.s: During pushback at ZZZ, the tug driver reported a tow bar breakaway. The Captain applied brakes to stop the aircraft, which was inspected per FOM procedures and returned to service for an uneventful flight to ZZZ1.

ASRSN:2153673.n: We were on the downwind leg for the approach to XXR. At 7000 ft ENG 1 surged multiple times with several loud bangs and then stopped. When the engined surged the only indication that I saw fluctuate was N1. The vibration indication stayed right around .4 and all other indications remained normal. Just before glide slope intercept the engine surged again disengaging the autopilot and so immediate actions items were performed. Thrust was reduced till surging subsided and again other than N1 fluctuating all other indications were normal and so the FO continued the approach and landed. After landing we noticed on the overhead panel that the ENG 1 CONTROL light was on. After parking at the gate I contacted Maintenance Control and gave a detailed debrief on what happened. No engine exceedences were observed on the displays. I made the necessary maintenance write up. I also contacted the Chief Pilot out of caution for a debrief. While being vectored on approach to XXR into ZZZZ, the number 1 engine surged. The engine indications were fluctuating rapidly while we felt momentary jolts and heard bangs from the engine. I began hand flying on the vector inbound and the captain completed the immediate action items. The captain continued to monitor the engine indications while I flew the aircraft. Soon after the jolts, the flight attendants called up to check-in since they felt and heard it in the back. The captain ran through the remainder of the engine surge checklist. Additionally, he input the single-engine missed approach procedure in the fix page for reference. We were cleared for the approach and we did not declare an emergency. After bringing the L engine thrust back to its engine indication's normal levels, the engine remained stable. We landed and during the taxi noticed the number 1 engine control light was illuminated. Once at the gate, the captain called Maintenance Control as well as the Chief Pilot and submitted a maintenance write-up. Station operations met us at the aircraft and were told of the write-up as well.
ASRSN:2153673.s: The crew experienced multiple Engine 1 surges with loud bangs and N1 fluctuations while on downwind for approach to XXR, causing autopilot disengagement. They completed immediate actions, stabilized the engine, and landed safely with the ENG 1 CONTROL light illuminated, prompting a maintenance write-up.

ASRSN:2153686.n: We were cleared into the gate from [Taxiway] 1. I taxiing and transitioning from taxiway to the west ramp taxi line (starting at spot XX). My attention was on taxiing from taxiway to our desired lane, when the First Officer alerted me to 'the van, stop, stop.' I can't be sure exactly what he said I quickly saw the vehicle approaching our path from the service road (west to east). I abruptly stopped the aircraft. Set the parking brake and called the Flight Attendant to ensure the Passengers and crew were okay which they were. The FO called ATC to notify them of the vehicle getting in our path. The van then backed up and allowed us to continue to the gate. After landing while taxiing on [Taxiway] 1 to line XX for gate XX a van failed to stop and drove in front of the aircraft from our right to left. I quickly stated van, stop, stop" and the Captain abruptly stopped the aircraft. The van also stopped and then backed up to behind their hold short line. After checking in with FAs we told ramp of the incident and continued to park without issue."
ASRSN:2153686.s: During taxi to the gate on Taxiway 1, a service van failed to stop and entered the aircraft's path from the right. The crew abruptly stopped the aircraft, verified passenger safety, and notified ATC before the van reversed and the flight continued to park without injury.

ASRSN:2153691.n: Received Dangerous Goods (DG) Summary and Final. Workload became high and did not get the DG acknowledgement code prompt submitted through ACARS before aircraft movement. High workload. Late into gate previous flight. Briefed and talked about Dangerous Goods (DG) Summary with FO, printed DG and Final. Did not send ACARS DG acknowledgement code until after departure. Had reviewed DG, aware of dry ice and location, but forgot to send DG acknowledgement code prior to brake release, due to high workload and time compression.
ASRSN:2153691.s: The flight crew reviewed the Dangerous Goods Summary but failed to submit the ACARS acknowledgement code before brake release due to high workload and time compression from a late arrival. The code was sent after departure, though the crew remained aware of the dry ice location.

ASRSN:2153703.n: ORCKA5 SID, passing approximately 2000 ft. we encountered wake turbulence that briefly required full right aileron to maintain course. About 10 seconds later we entered it again, so I directed PM to request immediate turn. Came left to 180, previous traffic was getting turns to right, and no further burbles. Reported this to LA Departure and continued flight. FO and I discussed any possible explanations other than wake turbulence and couldn't come up with any. No turbulence at all during the climb, and flight control page was all green. Plus, this was on a NEO. Only aggravating factor we came up with was that an A330 had performed a go-around on 25L just prior to us departing on 25R, so that seemed like the probable culprit.
ASRSN:2153703.s: Pilots on an A320neo encountered wake turbulence twice during the ORCKA5 SID climb near 2,000 ft, requiring full right aileron and an immediate left turn. They attributed the event to a preceding A330 go-around on runway 25L, as no other causes were identified.

ASRSN:2153711.n: On takeoff from runway 22R at EWR, flying the Newark5 departure, at 1250 feet and 2.3 DME on the localizer, starting the right turn back to a heading of 220, we passed a lighted UAS/Drone. The drone flew within approximately 50 feet of the aircraft passing directly off the left hand side and passing above the wing by an even smaller margin. ATC was alerted. Dispatch was debriefed after landing. Aircraft was visually inspected upon landing to ensure we did not hit the drone.
ASRSN:2153711.s: During takeoff from EWR runway 22R on the Newark5 departure, a drone passed within 50 feet of the aircraft at 1,250 feet. ATC was alerted, and the aircraft was visually inspected after landing to confirm no impact occurred.

ASRSN:2153746.n: Upon FO landing at ZZZ XXR, left brake pedal was fully pressed with no brake deceleration. Hydraulic system was normal, brake pressure gauge in green band. Decelerating past approximately 120 knots and losing rudder aerodynamic effectiveness aircraft started to slowly drift right off centerline with maximum manual braking. FO passed aircraft to CA who used gentle nose wheel steering below 100 knots to maintain centerline and max thrust reversers to 40 knots to exit taxiway 1. CA left rudder had limited travel and no braking effectiveness. Aircraft was safely taxied to the gate using only right side brakes. Maintenance was notified via ELB and verbally and aircraft was taken out of service. Taxi out of departure airport seemed normal due to steady taxi speeds. Likely cause was miss-rigged brakes and hardware missing on FO left brake pedal. Aircraft was a brand new 737 Max8. Second flight of the day, new AC, completed all preflight preparations/walk around / without event, noting during departure brief with CA it appeared to be a very new plane so it would be in good condition but also be prepared for unexpected issues that haven't been observed yet. I, FO, established as PF for this leg. Gate push, taxi to runway uneventful. Cleared to Lineup and wait on RWY XXR after straightening out and stopping CA gave me control of AC, I took over manually on the breaks not setting parking break and declared I have controls. CA reiterated I have controls, released breaks from their side. My, FO side, breaks held the plane in the stopped position with an observation that the left brake was depressed to the floor very slightly more than the right break which I concluded was normal slight difference usually due to not lining up completely straight or break pressure in both sides not being exactly identical. Did not seem to be an abnormal issue with the breaks. Tower cleared for departure. I released breaks to start take off roll was able to maintain centerline with no issues for departure. Continued to ZZZ uneventfully. I set auto brakes 2 due to having 12,000 feet available and the stopping distance for auto brakes 2 to be under 10,000 ft required. After uneventful touchdown, auto brakes and spoilers deployed as I maintained centerline with bottom of rudder pedals and deployed the reverse thrust. After a second I moved my feet up to the breaks in preparation to disarm auto breaks. I noticed immediately the left break was down forward, so severely, towards the floor. The right brake was in a standard position. The auto brakes were still operating when I made this observation. I then proceeded to disarm auto brakes per rollout SOP. Once I disarmed I noticed it was very challenging to press harder and harder on left brake and rudder and even though I was pressing much harder on the left break and rudder than the right, to what felt like full forward deflection, the AC kept departing the CL (Centerline) to the right. I mentioned to the CA very quickly immediately after I noticed it wasn't staying centered with a lot of left ruder/ break pressure that I thought something was wrong and to help me and that I was full deflection left rudder/ break. He took the AC at around 100-120kts, and the reversers were still deployed when I gave him controls. He was able to slow the AC with extended use of thrust reversers, prevent further departure to the right of CL and exit the highspeed taxiway to the left with very delicate use of the tiller at high speed. We noted hydraulic pressure and brake pressure in the green band. Taxied to the gate uneventfully. Upon Maintenance arriving they mentioned to us the left brake and tire temps were cool indicating to them they had not been used at all to slow the AC. They mentioned to us the right breaks had not overheated.
ASRSN:2153746.s: The First Officer landed a new 737 Max8 and found the left brake pedal fully depressed with no deceleration, causing the aircraft to drift right. Maintenance attributed the failure to miss-rigged brakes and missing hardware on the left pedal, resulting in the aircraft being taken out of service.

ASRSN:2153774.n: The first officer was performing his pre-flight and noticed that the electric stabilizer trim was not working. He tried different positions and we ended up calling maintenance. Maintenance came out, and after quite a bit of time of troubleshooting in the flight deck with breakers, they got it working. The mechanic stated that the 'fix' was to clean the electrical connectors on the electric stab trim motor in the empennage, because they were 'very greasy.' I asked if there was a repetitive inspection on these electrical connectors, and he seemed to laugh and then said no. My concern is that a build up of grease could create an in-flight problem.
ASRSN:2153774.s: The first officer discovered a non-functional electric stabilizer trim during pre-flight, prompting maintenance to clean greasy connectors on the empennage motor. The mechanic confirmed no repetitive inspection exists for these connectors, raising the pilot's concern about potential in-flight failures due to grease buildup.

ASRSN:2153871.n: Bag travelled on Aircraft X from SFO. Bag has a non-removable battery. Bag has been traveling from abroad from other airlines as well not being caught that it's a smart bag. Bag landed in ZZZ where we found out that we can't send it to passenger home so we had to send it via ground freight.
ASRSN:2153871.s: Crew on Aircraft X discovered a smart bag with a non-removable battery upon arrival at ZZZ. Because the item could not be returned to the passenger, it was shipped via ground freight.

ASRSN:2153907.n: During preflight review of aircraft status, aircraft was noted to have a deferred APU. Gate Preconditioned Air (PCA) was connected at the time, and was not satisfactory to cool down the cabin prior to boarding. Once an external air cart was connected to the aircraft for engine start purposes, the Captain and I elected to run both packs to cool down the cabin. Almost immediately I noticed an exhaust smell, which I believed was simply fumes ingested from the ramp area. As the cabin was cooling down, Maintenance was onboard resolving a pressurization controller issue. Once Maintenance work was completed, the Captain also noticed the smell and we both decided to shut down the packs until necessary to cool down the cabin with PAX on board. Approximately 2-3 minutes after turning off the packs, the cockpit began filling with visible smoke. The Captain, Maintenance personal, and I all investigated and could not determine the source. Maintenance inspected the Electronic Equipment (E/E) Compartment with no trace of the smoke. Captain then refused the airplane, and we deplaned the aircraft without further incident. We both visited the onsite clinic and removed ourselves from duty for the rest of the day.Cause: This issue couldn't have been mitigated by ensuring the APU was operating, especially during summer months in ZZZ. Was in preflight preparing for our flight to ZZZ1. The APU was deferred and crew ran the packs off the air start cart for approximately 20 minutes. We had an Estimated Departure Clearance Time (EDCT) so we shut down the packs and were using only preconditioned air to cool the aircraft for the 10 minutes prior to the event. At the same time we found an issue with the pressurization control panel and called ZZZ Maintenance. A maintenance technician arrived and resolved the pressurization panel issue. As he was getting ready to leave the Captain, First Officer (FO), and AMT noticed smoke of unknown origin in the flight deck. No smoke was noticed in the passenger cabin. The maintenance technician checked the Electrical Equipment (E and E) compartment for any indication of the origin of the smoke but found none.A maintenance supervisor was called and on his arrival the Captain refused the aircraft on the basis of smoke of unknown origin. The crew left the aircraft, the cockpit crew removed themselves from any further flying this day and reported to the medical clinic at ZZZ for evaluation. Examination by the doctor on duty showed both the Captain and First Officer fit for duty and both deadheaded to their home bases that evening.Cause: Possible issues with either the air-start cart, the air conditioning packs, or Preconditioned Air (PCA).
ASRSN:2153907.s: During preflight at ZZZ with a deferred APU, the crew ran air conditioning packs from an external cart while maintenance fixed a pressurization issue. Visible smoke of unknown origin appeared in the cockpit, leading the Captain to refuse the aircraft, deplane passengers, and have the crew medically evaluated.

ASRSN:2153953.n: This was day 2 of my trip with 3 legs that day. I was Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X. As we were on the arrival I briefed the Captain that we need to brief the land and hold short operations as they were in effect for ZZZ when I received the digital ATIS. Once we received the our runway assignment of XXL from ZZZ Approach, the Captain started to brief the ILS for XXL to me with the possibility of the hold short point of Taxiway 1 which had the available distance of 8600 feet. I sent landing data for Runway XXL and we had more than enough runway to accept to hold short point if ATC asked us. Coming in on the ILS XXL I was instructed to contact Tower at the final approach fix of ZZZZZ. After passing ZZZZZ I checked in with Tower and immediatley given a landing clearance of XXL and to hold short of Taxiway 1. I asked the Captain if he was comfortable with the LAHSO instruction and he told me that he was ok with it. I then proceeded to say clear to land Runway XXL hold short of Taxiway 1 and the Captain continued the approach to landing. I continued with my pilot monitoring (PM) thousand foot callout and my 500 foot callout as the Pilot Monitoring and everything was looking normal on the runway. At around the 100 feet from touchdown callout, the Captain noticed Aircraft Y in his line of sight on the runway. He stated there's an aircraft crossing the runway and he felt unsafe to continue the landing. I did not see the aircraft on the runway at the time the Captain called for and initiated his go around due to the pitch angle on the go around and he selected APR thrust to altitude. From this point he started doing is go around procedures while I was continuing to do my pilot monitoring duties. ZZZ Tower never stated if there they were having an aircraft cross the runway before our arrival when we received our landing clearance, nor did they tell us that any traffic was going to cross at the end of the runway for our situational awareness. After the go around, I cleaned up the aircraft, advised ATC we were going around do to aircraft on the Runway XXL. We followed ATC instructions after the go around and we were set up for Runway XY and landed without further incident. When ATC asked for our go around reason, the Captain told me to tell them that there was an aircraft on the runway and that he executed a go around. Once we landed in ZZZ, Tower told us there was a possible pilot deviation and to call them. The Captain called the Tower personnel once we arrived at the gate and started to deplane the aircraft. He was on his cell phone so I didn't catch all of the conversation but the Captain told me it was because we went around on a land and hold short clearance so he was arguing with the supervisor that if he felt the landing was unsafe due to an aircraft on the runway and we can always do a go around but they stated we have to land on a LAHSO clearance always and never be able to go around. The Captain wasn't agreeing with that statement and stated we will send a report out to the company to investigate further. I did review AIM 4-3-11 and it states, 'If a rejected landing becomes necessary after accepting a LAHSO clearance, the pilot should maintain safe separation from other aircraft or vehicles, and should promptly notify the controller.' This is exactly what we did for the go around.Cause: Captain felt unsafe with an aircraft on crossing the runway downfield after accepting the LAHSO clearance.Suggestion: If ATC told us there was traffic crossing the runway downfield past the runway safety area then I believe the captain would have continued the landing but since that didn't happen I am unsure if those would be his actions. I believe we should've been entitled to that information to see if there is an aircraft crossing the runway but I did not see an aircraft on the runway when the captain initiated his go around by the time he verbalized it to me. Inbound to ZZZ on the ILS XXL at ZZZZZ we contacted Tower and they cleared us to land. We didn't hear that they were going to cross aircraft at intersection 1." During the landing flare we saw Aircraft Y crossing the at end of the runway. I felt that during a rollout the aircraft at the end would be an issue of safety and I immediately executed a Balked Landing and we notified ATC. On the Climb out we were given left turn 180 and up to 3000 feet we complied with the instructions and got the Autopilot on. Then heading 160 and we were then told to contact Departure and Departure set us up for vectors for the visual XY. Once we landed on Runway XY and cleared the runway, and contacted Ground, Ground advised us of a "Possible Pilot Deviation" and gave us a phone number. Once we completed our Shutdown Checklist, I contacted the ZZZ Tower and spoke to Person A. Person A said he was issuing us a deviation because we accepted a LAHSO clearance and then we "Went around" and the Go around put us in close proximity of departures. He asked if I was familiar with LAHSO operations and stated I shouldn't have gone around. I then argued that pilots are always able to go around. I said "What if there was a vehicle, wildlife (deer) or anything else unsafe? Was I supposed to continue to land because I accepted a LAHSO clearance?" He then said "This will be reported and submitted for review." I then contacted Maintenance Control because we used APR thrust, called Dispatch to report as well. From my line of sight during landing, I also could not tell what intersection the aircraft was crossing and I was unsure so I elected to go around (balked)."
ASRSN:2153953.s: The Pilot Monitoring and Captain on Aircraft X executed a go-around during the ILS approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ after the Captain observed Aircraft Y crossing the runway despite a LAHSO clearance. The crew was later cited for a possible pilot deviation by Tower, who argued that a go-around was not permitted after accepting the clearance, contrary to the Captain's safety assessment.

ASRSN:2154023.n: On Day 0, FA 4 started smelling an acrid, musty smell in the cabin. She reported it to the Captain, right after the DH (Dead Head) Captain took his seat, while the Captain was talking to the DH Pilot. The Captain smelled the fumes odor. FA 4 thought that the odor was concentrated by 3L/3R doors, where the DH Captain's seat was located, but as she walked through the cabin, she noticed that the odor was strong and pervasive throughout the entire cabin, and passengers were complaining. Some of them knew it that it was fumes. FA 4 went to get FA 2 from the galley, and FA 2 also did a walkaround and smelled it. After returning to the galley, both FA 2 and FA 4's throats started being scratchy, and their sense of taste was also affected, as they tasted like a sweet, sour taste. FA 2 started coughing. We received an interphone call from FA 3, in the front galley. FA3 stated that passengers also noticed the smell and wanted to get off the aircraft. As we were talking, the Captain started making an announcement that everyone was supposed to deplane the aircraft. We all deplaned. We, the crew, all recognized the odor as the typical acrid, musty odor of toxic fumes, and we started feeling symptoms - headache, scratchy throat and eyes, compromised sense of taste, lightheadedness. Thank God the Captain was able to get us off almost right away! The plane was grounded, and we went to the hotel.As we went outside, our symptoms started to improve a little, but for some of us, some of them remained. The aircraft was supposed to be ready at XA:00 the following day. Captains were able to be released and dead head to ZZZ on Day 1. We went to the airport the same day, but the aircraft was still out of commission. The flight was cancelled. The passengers were irate and started vocalizing their anger. Some of them seemed to become violent. We were caught in the middle, with no place to go. We received notification that we were supposed to return to the hotel, but we couldn't even leave the area because the doors to Customs were closed, and we couldn't leave. The agents were dealing with the passengers, so they couldn't initiate the reopening of the doors to Customs. The passengers were getting closer and closer and were cursing at us. After a while, the agents were able to release us to Customs. Our new Captain from ZZZ1 told us that the aircraft would not have been ready the next morning either, informed the Company, and requested a new aircraft. The Company sent a new aircraft and new crews from ZZZ1. The Captain told us that he and the FO were supposed to ferry the broken plane back to ZZZ1, without passengers, on Day 2. We were assigned to work that flight, but there was no need for us to ferry on that flight because there weren't supposed to be any passengers. However, after hours and hours on hold with tracking, daily operations, and messages with a representative in ZZZ, Tracking would not release us and would not allow us to dead head back to ZZZ, as they heard that passengers were still listed on the ferry flight, on the broken plane.We went through a fumes event, and some of us were still not feeling 100% good, FA 4's bag was stolen at the hotel on Day 1. Even if the hotel security was able to retrieve it, we were no longer feeling safe at the hotel, we had no more clothes, only our uniforms, which still smelled like fumes, we ran out of medicines, and we just needed to go home. Thankfully, the next morning, another representative was contacted, and they started looking at our situation, and, finally, Tracking agreed to dead head back to ZZZ on a flight, the new segment which was created, with the new plane and the new crew, which were sent from ZZZ1, and our passengers from a flight.Suggestions: Not sure that fumes events can be prevented. The ZZZZ - ZZZ Captain heard our concerns and acted pretty quickly to deplane crew and passengers, and that was the key for us not to have more serious repercussions. As for our destinies after ourflight was cancelled, whenever crews are exposed to toxic fumes and experience a fumes event, they should immediately made go back to base, as they might need medical attention or just rest, as fumes can make crews sick, or tired. What happened to us was chaotic, as the FAs were forced to remain tied to a broken aircraft for no reason, since it was supposed to be ferried back to ZZZ1 with no passengers. There has to be better awareness and better coordination. Also, Tracking/Scheduling is the key here: they should be better trained to recognize the words 'FUMES EVENT' and, when they hear them, to return the affected FAs back to base as soon as possible, not to keep us hanging the way they did. This is inexcusable!
ASRSN:2154023.s: Flight attendants and the Captain experienced toxic fumes in the cabin, causing symptoms like scratchy throats and headaches, which led to immediate deplaning and flight cancellation. Subsequent scheduling delays prevented the affected crew from returning to base promptly, leaving them stranded with lingering health effects and safety concerns.

ASRSN:2154042.n: Was under ZZZ class B 1200 ft. ceiling near the waypoint. Holding 1000 ft. using autopilot.Uncomfortable because of the proximity to class B airspace, watching a line of weather moving across my front and my turbo controller apparently locked with the wastegate closed so my boost was much higher than normal. (Rotax 914 engine) I was cycling the throttle to diagnose the turbo problem at this time. Those distractions caused me to miss that I inadvertently touched the button for flaps. That caused the autopilot to start trying to pitch down but needed me to add trim down. This was yet another unexpected occurrence. This further distracted me and I missed that I was climbing rapidly. I realized I was already above 1200 ft. and could not understand what happened so rapidly. I pulled throttle to idle, disconnected autopilot and pitched steeply nose down. It took me several minutes to realize my flaps were at the first setting - which is for best climb. This is an experimental aircraft and I made an error placing the flap controller on the arm rest - so I wouldn't have to reach for it. I will need to build a 'gate' next to the buttons to prevent future inadvertent flap deployment. This has happened earlier in testing but I thought I had trained myself to keep my hand next to the buttons. I am happy to discuss further to clarify but bottom line, I believe human factors combined with poor placement of the flap buttons is the root cause.
ASRSN:2154042.s: The pilot of an experimental aircraft holding at 1000 ft near Class B airspace inadvertently deployed flaps while diagnosing a turbo issue, causing an autopilot pitch-down and rapid climb above 1200 ft. The pilot attributed the incident to human factors and poor flap button placement on the armrest.

ASRSN:2154049.n: I am a high time fixed wing ATP pilot that recently transitioned to rotorcraft and obtained my rotorcraft license. I flew to a location and landed in a yard the night before.
